Cost-Minimization of Endometrial Biopsy Strategies for Lynch Syndrome
Surveillance: A Decision-Analytic Model

**Précis:** [DRAFT, count words, limit 25] Combining endometrial biopsy with
an already-scheduled surveillance colonoscopy costs less than a standalone
office biopsy or operative dilation and curettage across a wide range of
assumptions and practice locations.

## Abstract

**Objective:** To estimate and compare the health-system costs of three
strategies for endometrial cancer surveillance in women with Lynch syndrome:
standalone office endometrial biopsy, operative dilation and curettage
(D&C), and endometrial biopsy performed during an already-scheduled
surveillance colonoscopy.

**Methods:** We built a decision-analytic, cost-minimization model from a
U.S. health-system/payer perspective, using Medicare-anchored allowed
amounts (2026 U.S. dollars). Each strategy was modeled as an initial
sampling attempt that either succeeds or fails and escalates to operative
D&C; the combined-biopsy strategy included only costs incremental to the
already-planned colonoscopy. Clinical probabilities were drawn preferentially
from Lynch-syndrome-specific literature. We conducted deterministic and
probabilistic sensitivity analyses (1,000 Monte Carlo draws), a threshold
analysis, a budget-impact analysis, a geographic sensitivity analysis using
real Medicare Geographic Practice Cost Indices and hospital wage indices
across four localities, and two supplementary clinical-outcome sensitivity
analyses testing the model's assumption of equivalent diagnostic
effectiveness across strategies.

**Results:** In the base case, combined biopsy cost an estimated $505.88 per
patient, compared with $764.93 for standalone office biopsy and $3,827.04
for operative D&C. Combined biopsy was $259.04 (33.9%) less expensive than
standalone office biopsy and was cost-saving in 82.0% of probabilistic
sensitivity analysis draws. Combined biopsy remained the least expensive
strategy across all four geographic localities tested, with its advantage
over standalone office biopsy widening from $209.77 in a low-cost locality
to $353.14 in a high-cost locality. Clinical-outcome sensitivity analysis
found combined biopsy carried substantially lower exposure to
D&C-rescue-driven adverse events than standalone office biopsy (mean 0.34
vs 2.11 events per 1,000 patients).

**Conclusion:** [DRAFT -- directly supported by data, no "further research
needed" language, per journal requirement] Endometrial biopsy performed
during an already-scheduled surveillance colonoscopy costs substantially
less than standalone office biopsy or operative dilation and curettage for
Lynch syndrome surveillance, and this advantage is robust to parameter
uncertainty and practice location.

## Methods

We conducted a cost-minimization analysis comparing three strategies for
endometrial cancer surveillance in women with Lynch syndrome: standalone
office endometrial biopsy, operative dilation and curettage (D&C), and
endometrial biopsy performed during an already-scheduled surveillance
colonoscopy (combined biopsy). The analysis took a U.S. health-system/payer
perspective, using Medicare-anchored allowed amounts (the Physician Fee
Schedule and the Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
Public Use Files) rather than hospital charges.^6^ All costs are reported in
2026 U.S. dollars; costs originally reported in an earlier year were
inflation-adjusted using the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index
for Medical Care.

A cost-minimization design assumes equivalent clinical effectiveness across
strategies -- specifically, that an adequate endometrial specimen provides
equivalent diagnostic information regardless of which strategy obtained it.
We did not extend the base case to a full cost-effectiveness or
cost-utility analysis (no quality-adjusted life-year axis, willingness-to-pay
threshold, or efficiency frontier). Instead, we conducted two supplementary
clinical-outcome sensitivity analyses that directly test, rather than merely
assume, this equivalence (described below).

Each strategy was modeled as a one-step decision tree: an initial sampling
attempt, which either succeeds or fails and escalates to operative D&C. D&C
itself was modeled as a deterministic reference arm with no escalation
branch of its own in the base case. The combined-biopsy arm was modeled
under an incremental-cost principle: because the patient is assumed to be
undergoing the surveillance colonoscopy regardless of whether biopsy is
added, no colonoscopy base cost, gastroenterology professional fee, or
baseline procedural sedation cost was charged to this arm; only costs
incremental to the already-planned colonoscopy were included.

Clinical probabilities were drawn preferentially from Lynch-syndrome-specific
literature. The office biopsy failure probability was pooled from three
studies confirmed genuinely specific to the Pipelle device by direct
full-text verification (22 of 166 attempts, 13.3%).^1-3^ The combined-arm
probability of escalation to D&C was the directly observed rate from a
10.5-year, 111-visit combined-screening cohort (2 of 111 visits, 1.8%).^4^
The combined arm's incremental procedure time (median 5 minutes, range 1-12
minutes) and incremental anesthesia requirement (no increase in dosing) were
drawn from a prospective feasibility study of the combined procedure.^5^

We conducted five complementary sensitivity analyses. First, deterministic
one-way sensitivity analysis varied each of ten parameters individually
across its low/high bound while holding all others at base case. Second,
probabilistic sensitivity analysis drew 1,000 Monte Carlo samples, with each
parameter sampled from a distribution matched to its evidence type (beta for
probabilities, gamma for costs, triangular for parameters whose uncertainty
is a structural or plausibility range rather than a formal confidence
interval). Third, threshold analysis solved for the parameter value at which
the combined strategy's cost advantage over office biopsy would be lost.
Fourth, scenario analysis modeled illustrative Medicaid and commercial
reimbursement and an alternative structural assumption about the combined
arm's preoperative visit. Fifth, budget-impact analysis projected annualized
savings across illustrative cohort sizes.

To test whether the base-case conclusion depends on national-average
Medicare pricing, we re-priced all three strategies at four localities: the
national average, a mid-cost state, a low-cost locality, and a high-cost
locality. Professional-fee components were adjusted using the Medicare
Geographic Practice Cost Index for the relevant procedure code and setting,
applying the standard relative-value formula (work relative-value units x
work index + practice-expense relative-value units x practice-expense index
+ malpractice relative-value units x malpractice index, divided by the
unadjusted total).^6^ The D&C facility fee was adjusted using the real
Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System wage index for the relevant
core-based statistical area,^7^ applying the labor-related-share formula
(labor share x wage index + [1 - labor share]) with the actual 60%
labor-related share finalized for the payment year.^8^ This geographic
analysis was kept deterministic rather than folded into the probabilistic
sensitivity analysis, since geographic variation is a question of whether
the conclusion generalizes to a different practice location rather than a
source of parameter uncertainty.

We conducted two clinical-outcome sensitivity analyses, computed from the
same probabilistic-sensitivity draws as the cost outputs. First, we
estimated each strategy's exposure to D&C-related adverse events (a
composite of uterine perforation, cervical false passage, and severe
hemorrhage, pooled from a cohort of 5,359 nonobstetric D&Cs)^9^ as a
function of that strategy's probability of ultimately requiring D&C, either
as the primary procedure or as a rescue procedure after a failed sampling
attempt. Second, for the office-biopsy arm, we estimated the probability of
a failed sampling attempt that is not rescued to D&C, combined with the
probability of cancer or precancer among women with a failed or insufficient
sample, drawn from a general (non-Lynch) postmenopausal-bleeding
meta-analysis.^10^ We were unable to construct a symmetric estimate for the
combined-biopsy arm, because the available combined-screening literature
reports a directly observed escalation-to-D&C probability but does not
separately report the fraction of combined-biopsy failures, if any, that go
unresolved without follow-up sampling; this limitation is addressed in the
Discussion.

We compared the model's cost estimates against three independently
published analyses as a validation check: a historical office-biopsy cost
anchor,^11^ a Medicare-payer-perspective decision-tree comparing Pipelle
sampling and D&C,^12^ and an independent U.S. economic model of office
versus institutional hysteroscopic surgery.^13^

All analyses were implemented in R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing,
Vienna, Austria) and are publicly available, with every model parameter
individually cited to its source. [Author: confirm final phrasing for a
double-anonymized submission -- the public repository URL and any
institution-identifying detail belong on the title page, not here.]

## Results

In the base case, combined biopsy cost an estimated $505.88 per patient,
compared with $764.93 for standalone office biopsy and $3,827.04 for
operative D&C. Combined biopsy was $259.04 (33.9%) less expensive than
office biopsy, and both office-based strategies were substantially less
expensive than D&C, which was more costly than both alternatives at every
facility fee tested, including a facility fee of $0.

The combined-vs-office cost difference was most sensitive to the office
biopsy failure probability (range -$144.23 to -$515.45 across its 10.3%-20.0%
bound) and the combined arm's incremental procedure time (range -$392.78 to
-$24.99 across its observed 1-12 minute range). At the upper end of the
observed time range, the combined arm's advantage over office biopsy
narrowed to $24.99 but did not reverse.

Across 1,000 probabilistic-sensitivity draws, combined biopsy had a mean
cost of $536.50 (SD $113.50) and office biopsy a mean cost of $678.20 (SD
$114.50). Combined biopsy was the least expensive strategy in 82.0% of
draws; D&C was never the least expensive strategy in any draw. Combined
biopsy remained the least expensive strategy as long as the incremental
colonoscopy-suite time stayed below approximately 12.7 minutes and as long
as the office biopsy failure probability stayed above approximately 6.5%.
At illustrative cohort sizes of 10 to 1,000 patients screened annually,
adopting combined biopsy over standalone office biopsy was projected to
save $2,590 to $259,043 per year.

Combined biopsy remained the least expensive strategy in all four localities
tested. Its advantage over office biopsy ranged from $209.77 per patient in
the low-cost locality to $274.33 in the mid-cost locality to $353.14 per
patient in the high-cost locality -- that is, the combined-arm cost
advantage widened, rather than narrowed or reversed, at the high-cost
extreme.

D&C-rescue-driven major-adverse-event exposure was substantially lower for
combined biopsy (mean 0.34 events per 1,000 patients) than for office
biopsy (mean 2.11 per 1,000), reflecting the combined arm's lower
probability of ultimately requiring D&C. D&C itself carried a mean
adverse-event exposure of 19.16 per 1,000. The office-biopsy arm's estimated
delayed-neoplasia risk (a failed sample not rescued to D&C that represents
cancer or precancer) had a mean of 1.52 per 1,000 patients. The
combined-biopsy arm's estimated delayed-neoplasia risk was 0.00 in all 1,000
draws by construction, not because the underlying risk is known to be zero
(see Discussion); we therefore report this as an exploratory,
office-arm-specific finding rather than a head-to-head comparison.
